```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",

imgt_dir <- path.expand(Sys.getenv("SIRUP_IMGT_DIR"))
has_trees <- nzchar(imgt_dir) && dir.exists(imgt_dir)
```

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  **Time:** ~15 minutes.<br>
  **Data:** example spatial MG thymus sections, bulk thymus BCR-seq, and bulk blood BCR-seq.<br>
</div>

Many studies have multiple spatial samples of the same tissue sections, or multi-modal AIRR-seq from the same patient.
Here, we will build and analyze a single SIRUP object that contains two spatial sections, bulk thymus BCR-seq, and
bulk blood BCR-seq. 

The SIRUP object contains
* `spatial`, a named list of spatial Seurat objects, one for each section.
* `receptors`, a named list of receptor tables, have one for each type of receptor. One table can hold all BCRs,
  including both spatial and bulk data. A `sample` column tells SIRUP which sample each row belongs to.
* Rows whose `sample` does not name a section stay in the table as non-spatial rows. SIRUP does not put them on a tissue, but clone calling, trees, and custom summaries can use them.

This page follows Figure 5 of the SIRUP paper. The MG thymus data come from a patient who had a thymectomy. Besides the two Visium sections, there is bulk BCR-seq of the thymus and bulk BCR-seq of blood, taken at the thymectomy
and 12 months later. The question is which clones in ectopic germinal centers (eGCs) also appear in the blood. An eGC is a site in the thymus where B cells proliferate and mutate their receptors.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  This page assumes a basic knowledge of the SIRUP object. To learn how an object is built, see `vignette("get-started", package = "SIRUP")`. To learn how the object works, see `vignette("sirup-object", package = "SIRUP")`.
</div>

## Get the example data

This page uses example files that are slightly too big to be part of the SIRUP package. This code
downloads them. Change `dest` to a folder you want to keep. The function skips files that are already there.

```{r download-data, message = FALSE}
extdata <- SIRUP::downloadSIRUPExample(
  dest = file.path(tempdir(), "SIRUP_example"),
  files = c(
    "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial_brighter.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds",
    "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv",
    "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz",
    "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
  )
)
```

## Load the samples

```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(SIRUP)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Load the two spatial Seurat objects and all of the BCR data.

```{r load data}
spatial <- list(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_spatial_brighter.rds")),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = readRDS(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_spatial_brighter.rds"))
)

# One AIRR file for each sample, with the compartment that the sample came from
bcr_files <- c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = "mg_thymus_slice1_bcr.tsv.gz",
  mg_thymus_slice2 = "mg_thymus_slice2_bcr.tsv.gz",
  bulk_thymus_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_thymus_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_thymus_2.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month0_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month0_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month0_2.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month12_1 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_1.tsv.gz",
  bulk_blood_month12_2 = "mg_thymus_bulk_blood_month12_2.tsv.gz"
)
compartments <- c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = "thymus_slice1",
  mg_thymus_slice2 = "thymus_slice2",
  bulk_thymus_1 = "bulk_thymus",
  bulk_thymus_2 = "bulk_thymus",
  bulk_blood_month0_1 = "blood_month0",
  bulk_blood_month0_2 = "blood_month0",
  bulk_blood_month12_1 = "blood_month12",
  bulk_blood_month12_2 = "blood_month12"
)

bcr_list <- lapply(file.path(extdata, bcr_files), airr::read_rearrangement)
names(bcr_list) <- names(bcr_files)

# Put all BCRs together
all_bcrs <- bind_rows(bcr_list, .id = "sample") %>%
  mutate(compartment = unname(compartments[sample]))
```

Then add the spatial IDs to the spatial BCRs and filter the BCRs to only include sequences that are productive and
have reasonable looking Vs, Js, and junctions.

```{r filter}
# Add a spatial id to the spatial data
spatial_bcrs <- all_bcrs %>%
  filter(compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2")) %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  )
bulk <- all_bcrs %>%
  filter(!compartment %in% c("thymus_slice1", "thymus_slice2"))

bcrs <- bind_rows(spatial_bcrs, bulk) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "IGH",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))

count(bcrs, compartment, sample)
```

Load in and filter TCRs.

```{r tcrs}
tcrs <- airr::read_rearrangement(file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_tcr.tsv.gz")) %>%
  mutate(sample = "mg_thymus_slice2", compartment = "thymus_slice2") %>%
  extractSpatialIds(
    id = "sequence_id",
    spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
    regex = ",([ACGT]{16})$",
    suffix = "-1"
  ) %>%
  mutate(sequence_id = paste(sample, gsub(",", "_", sequence_id), sep = "_")) %>%
  filterAirr(
    locus_val = "TRB",
    min_v_length = 250,
    min_j_length = 30,
    min_junction_length = 10,
    productive_only = TRUE,
    min_consensus_count = NULL
  ) %>%
  filter(!grepl("[^ACGT]", junction))
```

We add columns  `sample` and `compartment` to each AIRR table. We extract the barcodes from the spatial sequences and then filter.,
Make sure the `sequence_id`s are unique. The code adds the sample name in front of the `sequence_id`, because IDs may repeat
between datasets, and it replaces the comma with `_`, because dowser renames tree tips that contain a comma.

The section rows get a `sample` that matches the names of the `spatial` list. The bulk and blood rows have their own sample names and no barcode.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #9e584a; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #8b3620; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>WARNING</b> </p>
  Make sure that the `sample` column of the receptor tables matches the names of the `spatial` list for the spatial 
  receptor sequences. Also make sure that the `sequence_id` column is (1) unique across all samples, and (2) does not 
  contain commas to avoid problems with Dowser.
</div>

## Create a multi-sample SIRUP object

Pass `createSIRUP()` the named list of Seurat objects, and pass `receptors` a named list of receptor tables. The tables
are the slots `"BCR"` and `"TCR"`, and only the spatial section has TCRs. Pass the name of the `sample` column to
`sample_id`. All slots use this column.

```{r create}
sirup <- createSIRUP(
  spatial = spatial,
  receptors = list(BCR = bcrs, TCR = tcrs),
  spatial_id = "barcode_10x",
  sample_id = "sample",
  image_scale = "lowres",
  swap_coords = FALSE
)

sirup
spatialSamples(sirup) # Get the names of the spatial samples
```

Visium barcodes repeat between sections, e.g., `AAACAAGTATCTCCCA-1` exists in both. SIRUP matches each receptor to a 
spot by sample and barcode, so the two sections stay separate.

If the sections need different image settings, give named values: `image_scale = c(mg_thymus_slice1 = "hires", mg_thymus_slice2 = "lowres")`.

## Get one sample

The accessors (`getReceptors` and `getSpatial`) take a `sample_id` argument, and the receptor accessors also take a `slot` argument.

```{r accessors}
getSpatial(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1")
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, "mg_thymus_slice1", slot = "BCR"))
nrow(getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR"))
```

`subsetSIRUP()` returns a new SIRUP object with only data that matches the named sample, which here is `mg_thymus_slice1`.
The new object has only the spatial GEX data from the entry in the `spatial` list named `mg_thymus_slice1`, and only the
 BCRs that have `sample == "mg_thymus_slice1"`.

```{r subset-sample}
slice1 <- subsetSIRUP(sirup, sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1")
slice1
```

`mergeSIRUP()` goes the other way. It combines single-section objects into a multi-sample object, and it adds a sample
column with the names that are given.

```{r merge}
slice2 <- subsetSIRUP(sirup, sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice2")
merged <- mergeSIRUP(
  slice1, slice2,
  samples = c("mg_thymus_slice1", "mg_thymus_slice2"),
  sample_field = "sample"
)
merged
```

## Add ROI polygons for each section

As discussed in `vignette("regions", package = "SIRUP")`, we can add ROI polygons to the SIRUP object with `addPolygons()`.
Since we have multiple spatial samples, we pass a named (with the section names) vector of polygon files.

```{r polygons}
sirup <- addPolygons(sirup, polygons_path = c(
  mg_thymus_slice1 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice1_gc_polygons.csv"),
  mg_thymus_slice2 = file.path(extdata, "mg_thymus_slice2_gc_polygons.csv")
))

getPolygons(sirup)
```

Both files number their polygons from 1, so SIRUP adds the sample ID to each polygon ID, i.e., `mg_thymus_slice1::1` and
`mg_thymus_slice2::1`.

## Plot multiple spatial sections

Functions that create spatial plots for a multi-sample object return a list with one plot for each section.
Set `combine_sample_plots = TRUE` to get one combined figure, or pass `sample_id` to plot one section.

```{r plots, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 10}
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  title = c("AICDA, section 1", "AICDA, section 2"),
  point_size = 1.5,
  combine_sample_plots = TRUE
)
```

```{r plot-one, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5}
spatialExpressionPlot(
  sirup,
  features = "AICDA",
  assay = "alra",
  layer = "data",
  sample_id = "mg_thymus_slice1",
  title = "AICDA, section 1",
  point_size = 1.5
)
```

## Infer clones and trees across all samples

Infer clones for the entire set of BCRs, including both spatial and bulk datasets, using `updateReceptors()` with
`scoper::hierarchicalClones()`. Clones represent the set of B cells that are inferred to descend from a common ancestor.

```{r clones, message = FALSE}
sirup <- updateReceptors(
  sirup,
  scoper::hierarchicalClones,
  slot = "BCR",
  threshold = 0.1,
  summarize_clones = FALSE,
  nproc = 1
)
```

Phylogenetic trees show the evolutionary history of a clone. Each tip in the tree is one observed sequence. With SIRUP,
trees can include tips from all spatial and bulk samples. 

This guide uses clone 1045. It has sequences in spatial section 2, including ectopic germinal center (eGC) 5, in the bulk
thymus, and in the blood at both time points.

```{r pick-clone}
tree_clone <- "1045"
tree_section <- "mg_thymus_slice2"

getReceptors(sirup, slot = "BCR") %>%
  filter(clone_id == tree_clone) %>%
  count(compartment)
```

Next, make the germline of the clone with `dowser::createGermlines()`. The germline is the sequence of the unmutated
common ancestor, which roots the tree. As in `vignette("clones-and-trees", package = "SIRUP")`, building the germline
requires IMGT references. Set the variable `imgt_dir` to the folder that contains them.

<div markdown="1" style="background: #F7E5BC; padding: 12px; margin-bottom: 24px; line-height: 24px;">
  <p style="margin: -12px -12px 12px; padding: 6px 12px; background: #d6b676; color: #ffffff; font-weight: 700;"> <b>Note</b> </p>
  If you have not yet set up the IMGT references, see the [documentation](https://github.com/hoehnlab/airrblast) for the
  `airrblast` package and download and set up the IMGT references.
</div>

Keep `compartment` in `traits`, because the tree plot uses it to set the tip shapes.

```{r tree, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(sirup, dplyr::filter, clone_id == tree_clone, slot = "BCR")
tree_sirup <- updateReceptors(
  tree_sirup,
  dowser::createGermlines,
  slot = "BCR",
  references = dowser::readIMGT(imgt_dir),
  id = "sequence_id"
)
```

To build trees with Dowser, we need a formatted clones object. `formatSpatialClones()` wraps `dowser::formatClones()` 
but allows users to provide a SIRUP object, and it automatically places a `formatted_clones` object in the SIRUP object's
analysis slot. Then, we can call `getSpatialTrees()`, which wraps `dowser::getTrees()` but allows users to provide a SIRUP
object, and puts the trees in the SIRUP object's analysis slot. 

```{r tree-format, eval = has_trees}
tree_sirup <- formatSpatialClones(
  tree_sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  id = "sequence_id",
  traits = c("barcode_10x", "sample", "compartment", "polygon_id")
)

tree_sirup <- getSpatialTrees(tree_sirup, slot = "BCR")
trees <- getAnalysis(tree_sirup, "trees_BCR")
```

`plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` plots the tree on the left and the H\&E image of the section(s) on the right. Tips in the 
tree are plotted in their corresponding spots in the tissue if they are from the spatial data. The argument `shape_by`
sets the shape for each tip according to the provided column (here `"compartment"`), and `color_by` colors the tips by
cluster. `clusterTreesTips()` clusters the tips in the tree by genetic relationships in order to
provide visual clarity for paired plots. Here, `k = 6` splits the tree into six groups of tips.

```{r tree-plot, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
trees <- clusterTreesTips(trees, k = 6, id = "sequence_id", method = "monophyletic_clades")

pair <- plotSpatialCloneTreePairs(
  trees,
  object = sirup,
  slot = "BCR",
  id = "sequence_id",
  color_by = "tree_cluster",
  shape_by = "compartment",
  shape_values = c(
    thymus_slice1 = 21, thymus_slice2 = 21, bulk_thymus = 22,
    blood_month0 = 24, blood_month12 = 23
  ),
  polygons = TRUE,
  polygon_alpha = 0,
  polygon_color = "black",
  show_spatial_legend = TRUE,
  legend_theme = ggplot2::theme(
    legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7),
    legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(size = 8, face = "bold"),
    legend.key.size = grid::unit(0.3, "cm")
  )
)

names(pair)
```

In general, the `plotSpatialCloneTreePairs()` function returns a list of plots, one for each clone. If a clone has sequences
in multiple spatial samples, the list will have one element for each clone-sample combination, named `<clone>::<sample>`.
Each one pairs the full tree with the map of one section. The code below shows the section that holds the eGC tips.

```{r tree-plot-show, eval = has_trees, fig.width = 14, fig.height = 7}
key <- paste0(tree_clone, "::", tree_section)
if (!key %in% names(pair)) key <- tree_clone
section_pair <- pair[[key]]

section_pair
```



## Save and read the object

`saveSIRUP()` writes the object to a file. `readSIRUP()` reads it back and checks its structure.

```{r save}
path <- file.path(tempdir(), "mg_thymus.sirup.rds")
saveSIRUP(sirup, path)
readSIRUP(path)
```
